intro: The mug travels from a commercial focal point to a repeatable sign and a source of pattern.
alt: Four graphic compositions use an enlarged mug, repeated pictograms, interlaced ornament and a red circle.

variants.name: Plakatstil
variants.look: Silhouettes and broad blocks isolate one oversized product.
variants.history: Lucian Bernhard helped develop the German object poster, where a simplified product and its name carried the advertisement.
variants.when: Strip the composition down to a focal object readable at a glance.
variants.why: Untangled contours survive a brief glance or a distant viewpoint.

source.label: Neue Galerie · The Modern Poster in Germany

variants.name: Isotype pictograms
variants.look: Repeated figures establish a measurable rhythm across the panel.
variants.history: Otto Neurath, Marie Neurath and Gerd Arntz developed the Vienna Method, later known as Isotype, to make social statistics accessible.
variants.when: Use repeated equal units to communicate quantity or comparison.
variants.why: A repeated icon can be counted directly and compared by row.

variants.name: Wiener Werkstätte
variants.look: Checker frames and floral motifs organize figure and ground together.
variants.history: Josef Hoffmann and Koloman Moser cofounded the Vienna workshops to bring design to everyday objects and interiors.
variants.when: Design a family of related surfaces through a shared vocabulary of pattern.
variants.why: Repetition ties distinct objects together without requiring them to share a silhouette.

variants.name: Japanese postwar graphic design
variants.look: An oversized red circle intersects the figure in clean asymmetry.
variants.history: Postwar Japanese designers such as Yusaku Kamekura combined international modernist design with imagery suited to Japanese clients and audiences.
variants.when: Use a dominant geometric accent to organize varied imagery.
variants.why: One large geometric shape can anchor the eye quickly amid asymmetrically placed images.

prompt: Draw a single textless art comparison board for a museum-quality online art atlas. Layout is exactly four square cells in 2x2, edge-to-edge, no gutters or borders; precise, strictly equally sized cells. Order is left to right within each row, then next row. Each cell is a distinct style treatment featuring the same female executive from reference, in original new art. The reference image is for identity only: recognizable ash-blonde hair in neat low bun with four-color windowpane hair clip, black-rimmed rectangular glasses over blue eyes, charcoal sheath dress under fitted black blazer, azure pocket square and blue lanyard with blank ID badge, holding a white coffee mug with a little four-color tile mark. Change the actual render style rather than adding only backgrounds. Layout styles in order: Plakatstil: single oversized mug and executive as simple contours in black and tomato on cream, commercial lithography; Isotype pictograms: repeated small human icons in orderly rows, her icon holds a mug, red and black; Wiener Werkstätte: elegant black and gold checker framework, small repeating squares, ornate flower decoration around poised figure; Japanese postwar graphic design: meticulous photomontage profile intersected by a flat blazing red circle and navy oval in a crisply asymmetrical layout. No readable text, numbers, signatures, words, or extra panels.
